props.title: Flowers for Algernon

sections.content: Flowers for Algernon (2000) adapts Daniel Keyes' heartbreaking sci-fi novella with Matthew Modine delivering a powerful performance as Charlie Gordon. The film follows similar territory as Charly (1968), which earned Cliff Robertson an Oscar, but takes a more intimate approach to depicting cognitive enhancement and regression. Like Awakenings (1990) and Rain Man (1988), it grapples with questions of intelligence, identity, and what makes us human. The made-for-TV format allows for a slower, more faithful adaptation of Charlie's journal entries compared to the 1968 version.

sections.content: The film's themes of medical ethics and human experimentation connect it to other crucial sci-fi explorations like Gattaca (1997) and The Island (2005). The emotional core centers on Charlie's growing awareness of his previous limitations and the cruelty he faced, similar to the awakening consciousness depicted in Lucy (2014) and Limitless (2011), though with a more tragic trajectory. SUBHEAD: Intelligence Enhancement in Cinema

Films exploring cognitive enhancement often focus on the moral implications and personal costs. Limitless (2011) presents it as a Faustian bargain with pharmaceutical consequences, while Lucy (2014) takes it to superhuman extremes. Flowers for Algernon stands apart by emphasizing the human cost - Charlie's painful awareness of his inevitable decline mirrors themes in Still Alice (2014), where Julianne Moore's character experiences the opposite journey through early-onset Alzheimer's.
